title: Hypoparathyroidism: Protect Calcium Without Creating Hypercalciuria
bottomLine: Chronic hypoparathyroidism is low/inappropriately normal PTH with hypocalcemia after relevant causes are considered. Treatment balances symptoms and serum calcium against hypercalciuria, renal injury and overtreatment; acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is an emergency, while chronic therapy requires calcium/vitamin D strategy plus renal and urinary monitoring.
recognize: Perioral tingling, cramps, tetany, seizures and QT prolongation can occur with significant hypocalcemia.
Postsurgical disease is common, but autoimmune/genetic and magnesium-related causes also exist.
differentiate: Low calcium with high PTH suggests secondary response rather than hypoparathyroidism.
Severe hypomagnesemia can suppress PTH secretion/action and must be corrected.
assessment: Assess symptoms, prior neck surgery, magnesium, renal function, medications, pregnancy and adherence to calcium/active vitamin D.
workup: Confirm calcium status using corrected/ionized calcium as appropriate plus PTH, magnesium, phosphate, renal function and vitamin D context.
Use urinary calcium monitoring when chronic replacement can produce hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis.
management: Treat chronic disease with individualized calcium and active vitamin D therapy, correcting magnesium and other contributors.
Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium according to emergency protocol.
medicationSafety: Over-replacement can cause hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis and renal dysfunction even when serum calcium appears acceptable.
Thiazide or PTH-replacement strategies are specialist-directed when conventional therapy is inadequate.
counselling: Teach symptoms of both low and high calcium and why urine/kidney monitoring matters even when symptoms are controlled.
followUp: Track calcium, phosphate, magnesium, renal function and urinary calcium according to stability and therapy changes.
examTrap: Escalating calcium/active vitamin D solely to normalize serum calcium while ignoring rising urine calcium and renal risk.
oneLinePearl: In hypoparathyroidism, the goal is safe calcium—not the highest normal calcium.

title: Vitamin D Deficiency: Test and Treat When the Result Will Change Care
bottomLine: Vitamin D testing should answer a clinical question rather than screen every asymptomatic patient. Evaluate deficiency in people with bone/mineral disease, malabsorption, selected medications or other meaningful risk, then treat with an appropriate replacement strategy while considering calcium, renal disease and the underlying cause.
recognize: Risk rises with limited intake/sun exposure, malabsorption, bariatric surgery, CKD/liver disease, osteoporosis/osteomalacia and selected anticonvulsants or other medications.
Severe deficiency can contribute to osteomalacia, muscle weakness and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
differentiate: Low 25-hydroxyvitamin D reflects vitamin D status; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is not the routine deficiency test.
Bone pain/weakness can have many causes and should not be attributed to vitamin D without context.
assessment: Assess bone pain/fracture, falls, diet/supplements, malabsorption/bariatric history, renal/liver disease, medications and pregnancy.
workup: Order 25-hydroxyvitamin D when the result will change management and consider calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH and renal testing when osteomalacia/mineral disease is suspected.
Avoid indiscriminate repeated vitamin D testing once a stable plan is established.
management: Use guideline-consistent replacement and maintenance dosing individualized to severity, absorption and comorbidity.
Treat the cause when malabsorption, medication effect or other disease contributes.
medicationSafety: Excess vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria and kidney injury.
Granulomatous disease and selected conditions can alter vitamin D/calcium physiology and require specialist input.
redFlags: Malabsorption with failure of oral replacement
counselling: Review total vitamin D from supplements and fortified products and discourage megadose self-treatment.
followUp: Repeat testing only when deficiency severity, adherence, absorption or a therapeutic decision justifies it.
examTrap: Ordering 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D as the routine screening test for nutritional vitamin D deficiency.
oneLinePearl: For vitamin D status, test 25-hydroxyvitamin D when there is a reason to act on the result.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada endocrine/laboratory testing principles

title: Osteoporosis: Treat Fracture Risk, Not the T-Score Alone
bottomLine: Osteoporosis management is fracture-risk management. Prior fragility fracture, age, BMD, falls, glucocorticoids and other clinical factors determine treatment intensity; medication choice and duration must include renal function, administration feasibility, adherence and a plan for what happens when therapy is stopped.
recognize: A fragility hip/vertebral fracture can establish high fracture risk even before a DXA T-score is reviewed.
Falls, frailty and prior fracture often predict near-term risk better than BMD alone.
differentiate: Osteomalacia and other metabolic bone disease can mimic low bone density and require different treatment.
Low BMD without high clinical fracture risk may not require the same pharmacotherapy as recent fragility fracture.
assessment: Assess fracture history, falls, height loss, steroid exposure, smoking/alcohol, calcium/protein intake, renal function, menopause/hypogonadism and secondary causes.
workup: Use DXA and validated fracture-risk assessment where appropriate and investigate secondary causes when history/labs suggest them.
Vertebral fracture assessment/imaging is indicated when clinical risk justifies it rather than routinely for everyone.
management: Use exercise/falls/nutrition measures plus pharmacotherapy according to fracture risk and current Osteoporosis Canada guidance.
Choose antiresorptive or anabolic strategy based on risk, prior treatment and patient factors.
medicationSafety: Bisphosphonates require renal/administration review and long-term atypical femur/ONJ awareness.
Denosumab should not simply be stopped without a transition plan because rebound bone loss/vertebral fractures can occur.
counselling: Discuss absolute fracture risk, exercise/falls prevention and what the medication plan will be if therapy is interrupted or stopped.
followUp: Reassess adherence, fractures, falls and BMD at intervals that can actually change management.
examTrap: Stopping denosumab with no antiresorptive transition plan—or treating every DXA result without considering fracture risk.
oneLinePearl: Osteoporosis drugs are chosen and stopped according to fracture risk, not the T-score in isolation.
sourceBasis: Osteoporosis Canada Clinical Practice Guideline for Management of Osteoporosis and Fracture Prevention — 2023 Update

title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Explain the Bone Chemistry Before Calling It Osteoporosis
bottomLine: Low bone density, fractures or bone pain can reflect osteoporosis, osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism, CKD-mineral bone disorder, medication effects or other disease. Define the calcium-phosphate-PTH-vitamin D-renal pattern before assuming all low BMD is primary osteoporosis.
recognize: Osteomalacia can present with bone pain, proximal weakness, fractures and low phosphate/abnormal ALP depending on cause.
CKD alters phosphate, calcium, PTH and vitamin D physiology and changes interpretation/treatment.
differentiate: Osteoporosis is reduced bone strength with usually normal routine mineral chemistry; osteomalacia is defective mineralization and often has biochemical clues.
Primary vs secondary hyperparathyroidism requires calcium/PTH/renal/vitamin D context.
assessment: Assess fracture type, bone pain, weakness, diet, bariatric/malabsorption history, CKD, endocrine disease, medications and family history.
workup: Use calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH, vitamin D and renal studies when indicated plus DXA/imaging according to the clinical question.
Avoid shotgun rare-disease panels before establishing the basic mineral physiology.
management: Treat the identified cause—nutrient deficiency, endocrine disorder, CKD-MBD or medication effect—before applying routine osteoporosis therapy blindly.
Refer complex CKD/mineral or unexplained recurrent-fracture disease to endocrine/nephrology/bone expertise.
medicationSafety: Bisphosphonates/denosumab can be inappropriate or hazardous in selected untreated mineral abnormalities or advanced renal disease without specialist planning.
Correct clinically significant hypocalcemia/vitamin D deficiency before antiresorptive therapy when indicated.
redFlags: Advanced CKD with complex bone disease
counselling: Explain why the cause of weak bone matters because the wrong osteoporosis drug will not fix every metabolic bone disorder.
followUp: Track the biochemical abnormality and fracture risk after cause-specific treatment.
examTrap: Treating osteomalacia or CKD-mineral bone disease as ordinary osteoporosis because DXA is low.
oneLinePearl: Low BMD is a finding; mineral physiology tells you what kind of bone problem you are treating.

title: Pituitary Adenoma: Hormone Excess, Hormone Loss, or Mass Effect?
bottomLine: A pituitary adenoma can cause hormone hypersecretion, pituitary hormone deficiency or mass effect. Evaluate the symptom/hormone pattern systematically and treat sudden severe headache, visual loss/ophthalmoplegia or hemodynamic compromise as possible pituitary apoplexy requiring emergency specialty care.
recognize: Hyperprolactinemia, acromegalic features, Cushing disease, hypogonadism, central hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency can arise depending on tumour type/size.
Bitemporal visual-field loss, headache and cranial-nerve symptoms suggest mass effect.
differentiate: Medication/stalk-effect hyperprolactinemia differs from a prolactinoma.
An incidental microadenoma without hormonal activity differs from a macroadenoma threatening vision/pituitary function.
assessment: Assess visual symptoms, headache, menstrual/sexual function, galactorrhea, acromegalic/Cushing features, polyuria/polydipsia and adrenal/thyroid deficiency symptoms.
workup: Use targeted pituitary hormone evaluation and MRI when clinically indicated; formal visual-field testing is required when the lesion approaches/compresses the optic apparatus.
Do not diagnose hormone excess from a random screening value when formal confirmatory testing is required.
management: Treatment depends on tumour type: dopamine agonist for most prolactinomas, surgery for selected mass/functioning tumours, and endocrine replacement for deficiencies.
Pituitary apoplexy requires urgent emergency/endocrine/neurosurgical management including adrenal coverage when indicated.
medicationSafety: Before starting thyroid hormone in a patient with possible central pituitary disease, ensure adrenal insufficiency is considered because untreated cortisol deficiency can be dangerous.
Dopamine-agonist and other therapies require diagnosis-specific monitoring.
counselling: Explain which hormone axis and mass-effect symptoms are being monitored and when sudden headache/vision change is an emergency.
followUp: Track hormone status, MRI/visual fields and replacement needs according to tumour type and treatment.
examTrap: Starting levothyroxine for central hypothyroidism without first considering coexisting ACTH/cortisol deficiency.
oneLinePearl: Pituitary disease is three questions: excess hormone, missing hormone, and mass effect.

title: PCOS: Treat Reproductive Symptoms and Metabolic Risk Together
bottomLine: PCOS is a reproductive-metabolic syndrome diagnosed after appropriate exclusion of important mimics. Management should address irregular ovulation/endometrial protection, hyperandrogenic symptoms, fertility goals and long-term metabolic risk without reducing care to weight loss advice.
recognize: Irregular ovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology can contribute to diagnosis depending on age/context.
Insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea and increased diabetes risk are common comorbid concerns.
differentiate: Pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH and androgen-secreting tumours can mimic parts of PCOS.
Rapid virilization or very high androgens are not routine PCOS until dangerous causes are excluded.
assessment: Assess menstrual pattern, hyperandrogenism, pregnancy goals, medications, eating-disorder/weight stigma concerns, sleep apnea, BP, glucose/lipids and endometrial risk.
workup: Use cause-exclusion labs and metabolic screening appropriate to the presentation; ultrasound is not mandatory for every diagnosis, especially in adolescents.
Investigate rapid virilization/marked androgen elevation urgently.
management: Use cycle/endometrial protection, antiandrogen/contraceptive strategies when appropriate, fertility treatment when desired and evidence-based metabolic interventions.
Metformin and obesity pharmacotherapy are selected for appropriate metabolic indications rather than prescribed solely because the patient has PCOS.
medicationSafety: Antiandrogens require pregnancy prevention where teratogenic risk exists.
Combined hormonal contraception needs usual thrombotic/vascular risk assessment.
counselling: Use weight-neutral, non-stigmatizing counselling and address fertility and metabolic goals separately.
followUp: Track cycles/endometrial protection, metabolic markers and treatment goals over time.
examTrap: Diagnosing PCOS from ovarian morphology alone without excluding pregnancy, thyroid/prolactin or dangerous androgen excess.
oneLinePearl: PCOS care protects the endometrium and metabolic health while treating the patient's reproductive goals.
sourceBasis: Obesity Canada/Diabetes Canada metabolic guidance where applicable

title: Lipid Disorders: Treat Cardiovascular Risk, Identify the Extreme Pattern
bottomLine: Dyslipidemia treatment is risk-based. Established ASCVD and statin-indicated conditions deserve priority even when LDL is not dramatic, while very high LDL or triglycerides raise separate familial/pancreatitis questions. Use Canadian risk assessment and intensify therapy based on absolute risk and treatment response.
recognize: Clinical atherosclerosis, many patients with diabetes/CKD, abdominal aortic aneurysm and markedly high LDL are statin-indicated conditions under CCS guidance.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia raises pancreatitis risk and has a different immediate priority from isolated LDL elevation.
differentiate: Primary prevention depends on global cardiovascular risk and modifiers; secondary prevention is already high risk.
OTC fish-oil supplements are not interchangeable with evidence-based prescription lipid therapies.
assessment: Assess ASCVD, BP, smoking, diabetes, CKD, family history/premature disease, medications, alcohol, pregnancy and secondary causes.
workup: Use a lipid profile and Canadian risk estimator when appropriate; use ApoB/non-HDL-C and other risk markers when they add decision value.
Evaluate severe/extreme patterns for familial or secondary causes.
management: Use lifestyle support and guideline-directed statin therapy, adding nonstatin therapy when indicated by residual risk/treatment thresholds.
Treat severe hypertriglyceridemia with pancreatitis prevention in mind.
medicationSafety: Review pregnancy, interactions and clinically significant muscle/hepatic symptoms during lipid therapy.
Avoid labelling every muscle symptom permanent statin intolerance without a structured assessment.
redFlags: Very high triglycerides with abdominal pain
Severe muscle injury symptoms on therapy
counselling: Explain absolute cardiovascular risk and expected benefit rather than focusing only on one cholesterol number.
followUp: Recheck lipids after initiation/intensification to assess response/adherence, then at clinically appropriate intervals.
examTrap: Withholding a statin from a high-risk ASCVD patient because LDL looks only mildly elevated—or treating a low-risk modest LDL more aggressively than the high-risk patient.
oneLinePearl: Risk chooses the urgency; the lipid pattern refines the treatment.

title: Obesity Pharmacotherapy: Treat a Chronic Disease, Not a Willpower Problem
bottomLine: Obesity pharmacotherapy is evidence-based chronic-disease treatment used with health-behaviour and complication-focused care. Select medication according to obesity-related complications, contraindications, reproductive plans, adverse effects, access and patient goals, and continue effective therapy as chronic treatment rather than assuming a short course will permanently reset weight biology.
recognize: Obesity-related complications include diabetes, OSA, hypertension, MASLD, osteoarthritis, infertility and psychosocial impairment.
BMI alone does not capture all adiposity-related risk or treatment priority.
differentiate: Weight-loss medication for obesity is not identical to diabetes treatment even when some agents overlap.
Rapid unexplained weight change or active eating disorder requires a different diagnostic pathway.
assessment: Ask permission to discuss weight, assess complications, medications, eating-disorder symptoms, pregnancy plans, prior treatment, mental health, food access and goals.
workup: Screen for obesity-related complications and secondary contributors based on clinical risk rather than ordering broad endocrine testing without a phenotype.
management: Use current Obesity Canada pharmacotherapy recommendations and titrate an appropriate agent as tolerated alongside nutrition/activity/psychological support.
Consider metabolic/bariatric surgery pathways when benefits fit the patient's disease severity and goals.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy planning changes medication choices; anti-obesity pharmacotherapy generally requires stopping/avoiding agents according to product guidance.
Review GI, gallbladder/pancreatic, cardiovascular, psychiatric and drug-specific risks by agent.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing chronic-disease framing and discuss expected benefits beyond kilograms alone.
Explain that stopping effective therapy commonly permits weight regain because biology persists.
followUp: Track tolerability, function, cardiometabolic outcomes and patient-defined goals, not weight alone.
examTrap: Requiring a patient to 'fail lifestyle' before offering evidence-based obesity treatment—or prescribing a short course with no maintenance plan.
oneLinePearl: Obesity medication treats chronic disease biology; it is not a reward for perfect behaviour.
sourceBasis: Obesity Canada Adult Clinical Practice Guideline — Pharmacotherapy 2025 Update

title: Sodium and Potassium Disorders: Treat Symptoms, ECG Risk, and the Cause
bottomLine: Sodium disorders are interpreted through tonicity, symptoms, tempo and volume status; potassium disorders through level, ECG/neuromuscular effects, kidney function and cause. Dangerous electrolyte treatment is physiology-specific: symptomatic hyponatremia is not managed like chronic mild hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia requires separate myocardial stabilization, intracellular shift and potassium removal when indicated.
recognize: Severe hyponatremia can cause seizure/encephalopathy; overly rapid chronic correction can cause osmotic demyelination.
Hyperkalemia can cause weakness and malignant arrhythmias; ECG can be normal despite significant elevation.
differentiate: Pseudohyponatremia/hyperglycemia-related sodium changes differ from hypotonic hyponatremia.
Pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis must be considered when the clinical picture is discordant, but dangerous true hyperkalemia should not be delayed for repeated testing when evidence is convincing.
assessment: Assess symptoms, volume status, glucose, renal function, medications/diuretics/RAAS blockers, GI losses, intake, adrenal disease and ECG when potassium risk is significant.
workup: Use serum/urine osmolality and urine sodium selectively for hyponatremia classification; repeat potassium with careful sampling when pseudohyperkalemia is plausible.
Trend electrolytes frequently during active emergency correction.
management: Treat symptomatic severe hyponatremia with monitored hypertonic-saline protocols while limiting overcorrection.
For dangerous hyperkalemia, stabilize the myocardium when indicated, shift potassium intracellularly and remove body potassium while treating the cause.
medicationSafety: Diuretics, RAAS blockers, MRAs, NSAIDs and potassium supplements can drive abnormalities.
Insulin used for hyperkalemia can cause hypoglycemia and requires glucose monitoring.
counselling: Teach medication/sick-day and fluid guidance only after the cause is clear; generic fluid advice can worsen some sodium disorders.
followUp: Recheck electrolytes after medication/volume changes and ensure the cause—not only the number—has been addressed.
examTrap: Correcting chronic hyponatremia rapidly to a normal number or treating hyperkalemia with insulin alone without addressing myocardial risk and potassium removal.
oneLinePearl: Sodium is about brain/tonicity and tempo; potassium is about electricity and elimination.

title: Calcium Disorders: Confirm the Calcium, Then Follow the PTH Logic
bottomLine: Confirm clinically meaningful calcium abnormality using corrected or ionized calcium as appropriate, then use PTH and the clinical context to separate parathyroid from non-parathyroid causes. Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia and hypocalcemia are emergencies because neurologic, renal and cardiac complications can progress quickly.
recognize: Hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, constipation, weakness, confusion and arrhythmia; hypocalcemia can cause paresthesias, tetany, seizure and QT prolongation.
PTH should be suppressed in non-parathyroid hypercalcemia; an inappropriately normal/high PTH points toward PTH-mediated disease.
differentiate: Albumin changes total calcium without necessarily changing ionized calcium.
Malignancy, vitamin D excess/granulomatous disease, medications and immobilization are important PTH-independent hypercalcemia causes.
assessment: Assess severity/symptoms, volume status, kidney function, cancer history, medications/supplements, neck surgery, magnesium and vitamin D context.
workup: Confirm calcium and measure PTH early; add magnesium, phosphate, renal, vitamin D and cause-directed malignancy/endocrine testing based on the PTH branch.
Use ECG for severe symptomatic disorders or when QT/arrhythmia risk is relevant.
management: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia requires acute volume/etiology-specific management; severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored calcium replacement while correcting magnesium/other causes.
Long-term treatment targets the cause rather than chronic rescue dosing alone.
medicationSafety: Thiazides/lithium and supplements can worsen hypercalcemia; bisphosphonate/denosumab therapy can contribute to hypocalcemia in susceptible patients.
IV calcium administration requires appropriate formulation/monitoring and careful extravasation risk management.
counselling: Review all calcium/vitamin D products and explain why PTH determines which diagnostic branch to follow.
followUp: Trend calcium and the underlying disease/medication changes rather than repeatedly correcting the value without definitive diagnosis.
examTrap: Ordering parathyroid imaging before establishing whether hypercalcemia is PTH-mediated—or treating low total calcium without considering albumin/ionized calcium.
oneLinePearl: Confirm the calcium, then let PTH choose the differential branch.
